The formation reaction must start from the elements **in their standard states** — and for
iodine that is the **solid**, which is why the enthalpy of sublimation is given.
**The target reaction:**
½Cl₂(g) + ½I₂(**s**) ⟶ ICl(g)
**Step 1 — sublime half a mole of iodine.** I₂(s) ⟶ I₂(g) costs 62·8, so half of it:
½ × 62·8 = **+31·4 kJ**
**Step 2 — break the bonds.**
½ mole of Cl₂: ½ × 242·3 = **+121·15 kJ**
½ mole of I₂(g): ½ × 151·0 = **+75·5 kJ**
**Step 3 — form the I–Cl bond.** One mole of ICl releases its full bond energy:
**−211·3 kJ**
**Step 4 — add it all up.**
ΔfH° = 31·4 + 121·15 + 75·5 − 211·3
= 228·05 − 211·3
= **+16·75 ≈ 16·8 kJ mol⁻¹** ✓
The sublimation term is what the question is really testing. Leaving it out gives
121·15 + 75·5 − 211·3 = −14·65, which is option (b) — and that would be the answer if iodine
were a **gas** in its standard state. It is not; iodine is the only halogen that is a solid
at 298 K, so the extra step is unavoidable.
Note also that only **half** a mole of each element is needed, since one ICl contains one atom
of each.
∴ 16·8 kJ/mole.

pradeep|Chemistry|0|41|Pradeep Chemistry.s:
The scheme breaks the overall change into three steps, and by **Hess's law** the total is
just their sum.
**Step 1 — dissociation.** Half a mole of Cl₂ is split into atoms, so only **half** the
dissociation enthalpy is needed:
½ × Δ(disso)H° = ½ × 240 = **+120 kJ mol⁻¹**
**Step 2 — electron gain.** Each gaseous chlorine atom takes up an electron:
Δ(eg)H° = **−349 kJ mol⁻¹**
**Step 3 — hydration.** The gaseous chloride ion enters water:
Δ(hyd)H° = **−381 kJ mol⁻¹**
**Total:**
120 − 349 − 381 = **−610 kJ mol⁻¹** ✓
The one place to be careful is the **½**. The scheme starts from ½Cl₂, so only half a bond is
broken; using the full 240 would give −490, which is not offered — a sign the question is
watching for exactly that.
The large negative total is why chlorine is such a strong oxidising agent **in solution**: the
energy cost of breaking the Cl–Cl bond is more than repaid by electron gain and, above all,
by hydration of the small Cl⁻ ion.
This three-step breakdown is the **Born–Haber style** analysis of oxidising power, and the
same scheme applied to fluorine explains why F₂ is stronger still despite its *lower* electron
gain enthalpy — its hydration energy is much larger.
∴ −610 kJ mol⁻¹.

The answer is wanted **per equivalent**, and the concentration is given in **normality**, so
the two match directly.
**Step 1 — equivalents of acid.**
number of equivalents = normality × volume in litres
= 0·2 N × 0·400 L
= **0·08 equivalent**
**Step 2 — enthalpy per equivalent.**
ΔH = −(heat liberated) / (equivalents)
= −4·4 / 0·08
= **−55 kJ equiv⁻¹** ✓
The sign is negative because neutralisation is **exothermic** — heat is liberated, so the
enthalpy of the system falls.
Two conversions have to be right: 400 mL as **0·400 L**, and normality as equivalents per
litre. Using 400 directly gives −0·055; forgetting to divide at all gives −4·4.
It is worth noticing that −55 kJ equiv⁻¹ is **less exothermic** than the standard
−57·3 kJ equiv⁻¹ for a strong acid with a strong base, and that is exactly what should happen
for a **weak** acid: part of the heat released is consumed in dissociating the acid before
its protons can be neutralised. The difference, about 2·3 kJ, is the acid's enthalpy of
dissociation.
So the number is not merely an arithmetic result — it is chemically consistent with the
acid's being weak, as the question states.
∴ −55.

pradeep|Chemistry|0|49|Pradeep Chemistry.s:
Freezing is the **reverse** of melting, so its enthalpy change is the enthalpy of fusion with
the sign reversed.
**Step 1 — the magnitude.** The latent heat of fusion of ice is
**333·4 kJ kg⁻¹** (equivalently 6·01 kJ mol⁻¹, or about 80 cal g⁻¹)
so 1·00 kg of water involves **333·4 kJ**.
**Step 2 — the sign.** Melting **absorbs** heat, so freezing **releases** it. Energy leaves
the system, and the change of energy of the water is therefore **negative**:
**−333·4 kJ kg⁻¹** ✓
The question is almost entirely about that sign, since two of the options give the right
number and two the wrong one. The physical check is simple: a freezer has to pump heat **out**
of water to turn it to ice, so the water must be losing energy.
Options (a) and (d), 236·7, come from the enthalpy of **vaporisation** region or from a
misremembered constant; neither fits fusion.
Worth remembering alongside: the latent heat of **vaporisation** of water is 2260 kJ kg⁻¹,
nearly seven times larger, because boiling must break the hydrogen bonds completely whereas
melting only loosens them.
It is also why a pond freezing over releases a great deal of heat into the air — 333 kJ for
every kilogram of ice formed, which is what keeps the water near 0 °C for so long.
∴ −333·4 kJ kg⁻¹.

pradeep|Chemistry|0|50|Pradeep Chemistry.s:
The enthalpy of vaporisation is given **per mole**, so the mass must be converted to moles
first.
**Step 1 — moles of water.**
n = 80 / 18 = **4·44 mol**
**Step 2 — heat required.**
q = n × ΔvapH°
= 4·44 × 40·79
= **181·3 kJ**
= **1·81 × 10² kJ** ✓
The only real step is the mole conversion; using 80 directly would give 3263 kJ, which is not
among the options and so is self-detecting.
The figure is worth dwelling on, because it is the point of the question. Evaporating a mere
**80 g** film of water — a few tablespoons — takes **181 kJ**, and all of it has to come from
somewhere. On a swimmer leaving a pool it comes from the **body**, which is why the boy feels
so cold: 181 kJ is roughly the energy in a small snack, drawn out of his skin in a few
minutes.
The same mechanism is **sweating**, the body's main cooling system, and it works because
water has an unusually high enthalpy of vaporisation — a consequence of the hydrogen bonding
that must be broken to free each molecule.
Note that 40·79 kJ mol⁻¹ is the value at the **boiling point**; at skin temperature it is
slightly larger, around 44 kJ mol⁻¹, so the cooling is greater still.
∴ 1·81 × 10² kJ.

Let the bond dissociation energy of **XY** be a. The ratio XY : X₂ : Y₂ = 1 : 1 : 0·5 then
gives
BDE(XY) = a,  BDE(X₂) = a,  BDE(Y₂) = **0·5a**
**The formation reaction** makes one mole of XY from the elements:
½X₂ + ½Y₂ ⟶ XY
**Apply ΔH = (bonds broken) − (bonds formed):**
ΔHf = [½ × BDE(X₂) + ½ × BDE(Y₂)] − BDE(XY)
= [½a + ½(0·5a)] − a
= 0·5a + 0·25a − a
= **−0·25a**
**Set equal to the given value and solve:**
−0·25a = −200
a = **800 kJ mol⁻¹**
and since BDE(X₂) = a,
BDE(X₂) = **800 kJ mol⁻¹** ✓
The two places to be careful are the **halves** — only half a mole of each element is needed
for one mole of XY — and keeping track of which ratio belongs to which molecule. Here X₂
happens to equal XY, so the answer is a itself; in the companion question on the same page
the ratio is written in a different order and the arithmetic, though identical, must be
re-read.
A check: with a = 800, breaking costs ½(800) + ½(400) = 600 and forming releases 800, giving
ΔH = −200 ✓
∴ 800 kJ mol⁻¹.

pradeep|Chemistry|0|60|Pradeep Chemistry.s:
**Step 1 — identify the bonds on each side.**
O₂(g) + O(g) ⟶ O₃(g)
**broken:** one **O=O** bond in the O₂ molecule. The free oxygen **atom** has no bonds at all,
so it contributes nothing — that is the step most often missed.
**formed:** ozone is a bent molecule with **two** equivalent O–O bonds, each of average bond
energy x.
**Step 2 — write the enthalpy equation.**
ΔH° = (bonds broken) − (bonds formed)
−107·2 = 498·8 − 2x
**Step 3 — solve.**
2x = 498·8 + 107·2
2x = 606·0
x = **303 kJ mol⁻¹** ✓ (the option gives 302·6, the same value to the accuracy of the data)
The factor of **2** is what decides the answer: counting only one bond in ozone gives
606 kJ mol⁻¹, which is option (b) and is placed there for exactly that mistake.
The result is chemically revealing. Each O–O bond in ozone, at about 303 kJ mol⁻¹, is much
**weaker** than the 498·8 kJ mol⁻¹ double bond in O₂ — consistent with ozone's resonance
structure, in which the two bonds are intermediate between single and double, with a bond
order of 1·5. That weakness is why ozone is so reactive and decomposes readily back to O₂.
∴ 302·6 kJ mol⁻¹.

**Step 1 — the reaction and the bonds involved.**
H₂(g) + O₂(g) ⟶ H₂O₂(g)
Hydrogen peroxide is **H–O–O–H**: two **O–H** bonds and one **O–O** single bond.
**Step 2 — bonds broken (reactants).**
one H–H: **438**
one O=O: **498**
total = **936 kJ**
**Step 3 — bonds formed (product).**
two O–H: 2 × 464 = **928**
one O–O: **138**
total = **1066 kJ**
**Step 4 — subtract.**
ΔH° = 936 − 1066 = **−130 kJ mol⁻¹** ✓
The structure of H₂O₂ is the thing to get right. Writing it with an O=O double bond, or
forgetting the O–O single bond altogether, changes the answer completely — using only the
two O–H bonds gives 936 − 928 = +8 kJ.
Note that the **O–O single bond is remarkably weak**, 138 kJ mol⁻¹, far weaker than C–C at
348. The reason is repulsion between the lone pairs on the two adjacent oxygen atoms. That
weakness is why hydrogen peroxide decomposes so readily to water and oxygen, and why it must
be stored in dark bottles away from catalysts such as dust or metal ions.
The negative ΔH confirms H₂O₂ is stable with respect to its elements, even though it is
unstable with respect to H₂O + ½O₂.
∴ −130.

The two quantities start from **different physical states**, and that is the whole question.
**Bond enthalpy, y.** This refers to breaking the bond in the **gaseous** molecule:
Br₂(**g**) ⟶ 2Br(g),  ΔH = y
**Enthalpy of atomisation, x.** This is the enthalpy needed to convert the substance **in its
standard state** into gaseous atoms. Bromine's standard state is the **liquid**, so the path
has two stages:
Br₂(**l**) ⟶ Br₂(g),  ΔH = ΔvapH
Br₂(g) ⟶ 2Br(g),  ΔH = y
Adding them,
**x = ΔvapH + y**
Since vaporisation always costs energy, ΔvapH is positive, and therefore
**x > y** ✓
For bromine the numbers are ΔvapH ≈ 30 kJ mol⁻¹ and y ≈ 193 kJ mol⁻¹, giving x ≈ 223 kJ mol⁻¹.
Note that for **chlorine** the two would be **equal**, because Cl₂ is already a gas at 298 K
and no vaporisation step is needed — x = y there. Bromine is the odd case precisely because
it is the only halogen that is a liquid at room temperature, and the question depends on
knowing that.
For **iodine**, a solid, the gap is larger still: x = ΔsubH + y.
∴ x > y.

Take the two signs separately for
2Cl(g) ⟶ Cl₂(g)
**The enthalpy.** This reaction **forms** a bond: two free chlorine atoms join to give a Cl–Cl
bond. Bond formation always **releases** energy — it is the exact reverse of bond
dissociation, which costs 242 kJ mol⁻¹. So
**ΔrH = −242 kJ mol⁻¹ < 0** ✓
**The entropy.** Count the moles of **gas**:
left: **2** mol of gas
right: **1** mol of gas
Two independent particles become one, so the system has fewer ways to arrange itself — fewer
translational microstates — and the disorder falls:
**ΔrS < 0** ✓
So ΔrH < 0 and ΔrS < 0, which is option **(c)**.
The general rule worth carrying away: for a gas-phase reaction the sign of ΔS follows the
**change in the number of gas molecules**, and the sign of ΔH follows whether bonds are
formed or broken on balance.
Since ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, a reaction with both terms negative is spontaneous at **low**
temperature and becomes non-spontaneous at high temperature — which is why chlorine atoms
recombine readily in the cold but Cl₂ dissociates when strongly heated or illuminated.
∴ ΔrH < 0 and ΔrS < 0.

pradeep|Chemistry|0|67|Pradeep Chemistry.s:
For the **isothermal reversible** expansion of an ideal gas the entropy change is
**ΔS = nR ln(V₂/V₁)**
**Step 1 — the volume ratio.**
V₂/V₁ = 100 / 10 = **10**
**Step 2 — substitute.**
ΔS = 2 × 8·314 × ln 10
= 2 × 8·314 × 2·303
= **38·3 J K⁻¹** ✓
(Equivalently, using base-ten logarithms, ΔS = 2·303 nR log(V₂/V₁) = 2·303 × 2 × 8·314 × 1.)
The temperature of 27 °C does **not** enter the calculation. The process is isothermal, so T
cancels: the formula depends only on the volume ratio and the number of moles. The
temperature is given to establish that the process *is* isothermal, nothing more.
The sign is **positive**, as it must be — the gas now has a larger volume to move in, so there
are more accessible microstates and the entropy rises.
Where the formula comes from: for an isothermal ideal-gas expansion ΔU = 0, so q(rev) = −w =
nRT ln(V₂/V₁), and ΔS = q(rev)/T gives nR ln(V₂/V₁), with the T cancelling.
The factor **ln 10 = 2·303** is worth recognising on sight; it turns the whole calculation
into 2 × 8·314 × 2·303.
∴ 38·3 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.

pradeep|Chemistry|0|68|Pradeep Chemistry.s:
Two words in the question do all the work: **insulated** and **suddenly**.
**'Insulated'** means no heat can leave, so the vessel is an **isolated system** — the system
is effectively the whole universe for this change.
**'Suddenly freezes'** describes supercooled water at −10 °C crystallising spontaneously. A
spontaneous change is an **irreversible** one.
The second law says that for any **irreversible** process in an **isolated** system the total
entropy must **increase**:
**ΔS > 0** ✓
So the entropy of the system **increases**.
At first this looks wrong, since freezing orders the molecules and ought to lower the
entropy. It would — if the freezing happened reversibly at 0 °C with the heat carried away.
But here the latent heat released cannot escape: it stays inside and **warms** the contents
back up towards 0 °C. The entropy gained by that warming is larger than the entropy lost in
ordering the molecules, and the net change is positive.
That is precisely why supercooled water freezes spontaneously at −10 °C and not at, say,
+5 °C — the second law permits it only below the melting point.
Note the contrast with ordinary freezing at 0 °C in a freezer, where heat **does** leave and
the water's own entropy falls.
∴ increases.

Note: the printed key gives (c), zero. A zero entropy change would mean the process is
reversible, whereas the sudden freezing of supercooled water in an insulated vessel is
irreversible and must increase the entropy; the key is wrong and has been corrected to (b).

pradeep|Chemistry|0|75|Pradeep Chemistry.s:
Both **S** and **ΔS** depend on temperature, and the reasons are worth separating.
**S depends on temperature.** The absolute entropy of a substance rises as it is heated:
dS = C(p) dT / T
so heating from T₁ to T₂ adds C(p) ln(T₂/T₁). Physically, a warmer substance has more
thermal energy to distribute among its molecules, so more microstates are accessible. At 0 K
a perfect crystal has S = 0 (third law), and S climbs steadily from there, with jumps at each
phase change.
**ΔS also depends on temperature.** This is the half that is easy to doubt. ΔS between two
states is the difference of two quantities that each vary with T, and they do **not** vary in
step — the reactants and products generally have different heat capacities. The relation is
ΔS(T₂) = ΔS(T₁) + ΔC(p) ln(T₂/T₁)
(Kirchhoff's equation for entropy), so unless ΔC(p) happens to be zero, ΔS changes with
temperature too.
So **both** are functions of temperature ✓ — option (b).
Options (a) and (d) each hold one of them fixed, and (c) holds both fixed, which would make
entropy independent of heating altogether — contradicting the third law's starting point of
S = 0 at 0 K.
∴ both ΔS and S are functions of temperature.

pradeep|Chemistry|0|76|Pradeep Chemistry.s:
Entropy falls whenever a system becomes **more ordered** — in practice, whenever gas is lost
or a liquid becomes a solid. Take each process.
**(A) Freezing of water to ice at 0 °C** — liquid ⟶ solid. The molecules lock into a lattice,
so the disorder falls. **ΔS < 0** ✓
**(B) Freezing of water to ice at −10 °C** — the same phase change, so again the water's own
entropy **decreases**. **ΔS < 0** ✓
**(C) N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⟶ 2NH₃(g)** — **4** moles of gas become **2**. Fewer gas molecules means
far fewer accessible microstates. **ΔS < 0** ✓
**(D) Adsorption of CO(g) on a lead surface** — a freely moving gas is pinned to a surface,
losing almost all its translational freedom. Adsorption is **always** accompanied by a
decrease in entropy. **ΔS < 0** ✓
**(E) Dissolution of NaCl in water** — the ordered crystal lattice breaks up and the ions
disperse through the solvent. **ΔS > 0** ✗ this one **increases**
So entropy decreases in **(A), (B), (C) and (D)** — option (a).
The general signals to look for: **gas disappearing** (C, D) and **freezing or
crystallising** (A, B) lower the entropy; **melting, boiling, dissolving** and any increase
in the number of gas molecules raise it.
Note that (D) is also why adsorption must be **exothermic** to happen at all: with ΔS
negative, ΔG = ΔH − TΔS can only be negative if ΔH is sufficiently negative.
∴ (A), (B), (C) and (D) only.
